companionQuestions.prompt: A car slows uniformly from 24 to 18 m/s over 3.00 s. Find the distance in that interval.
companionQuestions.asking: Find how far the car moves while its speed changes.

clues.explanation: Acceleration opposes the moving object while it slows. Its starting velocity is positive on this axis, so braking acceleration is negative.
“Uniformly” means the acceleration is constant during this interval. That is why the average of the starting and ending velocities can be used.

steps.title: Write the known values
steps.text: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 24 m/s; vf = 18 m/s; Δt = 3.00 s.

steps.title: Choose the relationship
steps.text: Δx = ((vi + vf) / 2) Δt

hints: With constant acceleration, velocity changes evenly. Its average is halfway between the signed starting and ending velocities. Multiply that average velocity by elapsed time to get displacement.
Keep the chosen axis through the substitution; write the final vector direction in words.
companionQuestions.example:
Δd = ((vi + vf) / 2) × Δt
Δd = ((24 + 18) / 2) × 3.00
Signed calculation: 63 m. Final: 63 m.

repair.prompt: For uniform acceleration, which velocity belongs in distance = average velocity × time?
repair.explanation: Find the average of the initial and final velocities first. With constant acceleration, distance equals this average velocity times elapsed time.

answer.reasoning: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 24 m/s; vf = 18 m/s; Δt = 3.00 s. With constant acceleration, velocity changes evenly. Its average is halfway between the signed starting and ending velocities. Multiply that average velocity by elapsed time to get displacement. Δd = 63 m before final rounding. Final magnitude: 63 m. The stated measurements limit this result to 2 significant figures. For a velocity difference, subtract first using the least decimal place; then apply the multiply/divide rule. Rest/stop zeros, ½ and unit conversions are exact. Keep extra digits until the last line.
answer.commonMistake: Using only the final speed for the whole interval instead of averaging the initial and final speeds.

companionQuestions.prompt: A car begins at 17 m/s and accelerates forward at 3.0 m/s² for 4.0 s. Find its final speed.

steps.title: Write the known values
steps.text: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 17 m/s; a = 3.0 m/s²; Δt = 4.0 s.

steps.title: Choose the relationship
steps.text: vf = vi + aΔt

hints: Acceleration times elapsed time gives the change in velocity. Add that change to the starting velocity to get the ending velocity.
Keep the chosen axis through the substitution; write the final vector direction in words.
companionQuestions.example:
vf = vi + a × Δt
v𝒇 = 17 + 3.0 × 4.0
Signed calculation: 29 m/s. Final: 29 m/s forward.

repair.prompt: In vf = vi + aΔt, what does aΔt represent?
repair.explanation: The acceleration term aΔt is the change in velocity. Add it to the initial velocity, using one positive direction consistently.

answer.reasoning: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 17 m/s; a = 3.0 m/s²; Δt = 4.0 s. Acceleration times elapsed time gives the change in velocity. Add that change to the starting velocity to get the ending velocity. vf = 29 m/s before final rounding. Final magnitude: 29 m/s forward. The stated measurements limit this result to 2 significant figures. For a velocity difference, subtract first using the least decimal place; then apply the multiply/divide rule. Rest/stop zeros, ½ and unit conversions are exact. Keep extra digits until the last line.
answer.commonMistake: Forgetting the initial velocity, or assuming velocity and acceleration always point in the same direction.

companionQuestions.prompt: A car moving at 24 m/s stops after travelling 196 m. Find the magnitude of its deceleration.

a = (0² − 24²) / (2 × 196)

answer.reasoning: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 24 m/s; vf = 0 m/s; Δd = 196 m. This connects the two velocities, acceleration and displacement. Time is not in it, so you can solve without knowing how long the motion takes. a = -1.469388 m/s² before final rounding. Final magnitude: 1.5 m/s². The stated measurements limit this result to 2 significant figures. For a velocity difference, subtract first using the least decimal place; then apply the multiply/divide rule. Rest/stop zeros, ½ and unit conversions are exact. Keep extra digits until the last line.

companionQuestions.prompt: Explain distance and displacement with an example where they differ.

steps.title: Count the path
steps.text: For a walk 5 m right then 8 m left, distance counts both parts regardless of direction.

steps.title: Compare finish with start
steps.text: Right is positive. Add the signed changes: +5 + (−8) = −3 m. The finish is left of the start.

steps.title: State the distinction
steps.text: Distance is a scalar path length. Displacement is a vector change in position. An out-and-back trip can have nonzero distance and zero displacement.

hints: For a walk 5 m right then 8 m left, distance counts both parts regardless of direction.
Right is positive. Add the signed changes: +5 + (−8) = −3 m. The finish is left of the start.

Δd = −3 m → 3 m left.
Distance: magnitude. Displacement: magnitude and direction.

repair.prompt: An out-and-back walk ends at its start. Its displacement is…
repair.explanation: Distance counts the whole path. Displacement compares the finish with the start, including direction.

checklist: Distance: magnitude. Displacement: magnitude and direction.

steps.title: Read the vertical axis
steps.text: On a position–time graph, a horizontal line stays at the same position while time passes.

steps.title: Calculate its slope
steps.text: There is no change in position, so rise is zero. Dividing zero by elapsed time gives zero velocity.

steps.title: Describe the motion
steps.text: The object is stopped relative to this origin. A horizontal velocity–time line would have a different meaning, so the axis matters.

hints: On a position–time graph, a horizontal line stays at the same position while time passes.
There is no change in position, so rise is zero. Dividing zero by elapsed time gives zero velocity.
companionQuestions.example:
Position is constant.
v = Δd/Δt = 0 m/s.
The object is at rest.

repair.prompt: A horizontal line above zero on a velocity–time graph means…
repair.explanation: Read the axes first. Position–time slope is velocity. Velocity–time slope is acceleration. Signed area on velocity–time gives displacement.

steps.title: Choose the north axis
steps.text: Take north as positive. The car’s northward velocity is positive; the negative acceleration points south.

steps.title: Explain what changes
steps.text: Southward acceleration removes northward velocity each second, so the car slows while it is still moving north.

steps.text: If that acceleration continues after v reaches zero, the car reverses and gains southward speed. The wording does not give a duration, so do not invent a stopping time.

steps.text: Positive slope means forward motion; zero slope means rest; negative slope means returning. No durations or speeds are specified, so this is a qualitative sketch.

companionQuestions.prompt: What does position–time slope represent?

clues.explanation: Position is on the vertical axis and time is on the horizontal axis.

steps.title: Use the axes
steps.text: Rise is change in position; run is elapsed time. Their ratio is velocity.

steps.title: Keep direction
steps.text: A negative slope means motion in the negative direction. A horizontal position line means zero velocity.

steps.title: Distinguish average and instantaneous
steps.text: A line through two readings gives average velocity over that interval. A tangent gives velocity at one instant.

hints: Rise is change in position; run is elapsed time. Their ratio is velocity.
A negative slope means motion in the negative direction. A horizontal position line means zero velocity.
companionQuestions.example:
Slope = Δd/Δt = v.
Slope unit: m/s.
Secant: interval average; tangent: instantaneous velocity.

repair.prompt: Which change is on the vertical axis of a position–time graph?
repair.explanation: Slope is change in position divided by elapsed time: velocity. The sign of the slope gives direction.

answer.reasoning: Slope = Δd/Δt = v. Slope unit: m/s. Secant: interval average; tangent: instantaneous velocity.
answer.commonMistake: Reading the graph height as velocity, or using area when the question asks for position–time slope.

checklist: Secant: interval average; tangent: instantaneous velocity.

companionQuestions.prompt: What does velocity–time slope represent?

clues.explanation: Divide the change in velocity by the time interval.

steps.title: Use the axes
steps.text: Rise is the change in velocity, not the velocity itself. Run is elapsed time.

steps.title: Follow units
steps.text: Metres per second divided by seconds gives metres per second squared.

steps.title: Read the sign
steps.text: An upward slope is positive acceleration even below the time axis. A horizontal velocity line is zero acceleration.

hints: Rise is the change in velocity, not the velocity itself. Run is elapsed time.

Slope tells acceleration; vertical position tells velocity direction.

repair.prompt: What change belongs on top in velocity–time slope?
repair.explanation: Velocity–time slope is acceleration. Subtract velocities at two points, then divide by their time difference.

answer.reasoning: Slope = (vf − vi)/Δt = a. Slope unit: m/s². Slope tells acceleration; vertical position tells velocity direction.
answer.commonMistake: Using the final velocity alone instead of the velocity change, or mixing slope with area.

checklist: Slope tells acceleration; vertical position tells velocity direction.

companionQuestions.prompt: What does signed velocity–time area represent?

steps.title: Use area rather than slope
steps.text: Each thin time strip contributes velocity × elapsed time. Adding the strips gives displacement.

steps.title: Keep the sign of each region
steps.text: Area above zero velocity is positive; area below zero is negative. Add signed areas to find displacement.

steps.title: Separate distance
steps.text: Distance adds the magnitudes of those areas, so opposite-direction parts do not cancel.

hints: Each thin time strip contributes velocity × elapsed time. Adding the strips gives displacement.
Area above zero velocity is positive; area below zero is negative. Add signed areas to find displacement.

Δd = signed area under the velocity–time graph.

repair.prompt: What does area under a velocity–time graph give?
repair.explanation: The area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement. Split the interval into rectangles and triangles with their signs.

hints: The first term accounts for the starting velocity. The second adds the effect of accelerating during that time. If it starts from rest, the first term is zero.
Keep the chosen axis through the substitution; write the final vector direction in words.
companionQuestions.example:
Δd = vi × Δt + ½ × a × Δt²
Δd = 0 × 4.0 + ½ × 3.5 × 4.0²
Signed calculation: 28 m. Final: 28 m.

repair.prompt: Which term contains time squared in the displacement equation?
repair.explanation: Use Δx = viΔt + ½aΔt². Square elapsed time in the acceleration term, then add the initial-velocity term with its sign.

answer.reasoning: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 0 m/s; a = 3.5 m/s²; Δt = 4.0 s. The first term accounts for the starting velocity. The second adds the effect of accelerating during that time. If it starts from rest, the first term is zero. Δd = 28 m before final rounding. Final answer: 28 m. The stated measurements limit this result to 2 significant figures. For a velocity difference, subtract first using the least decimal place; then apply the multiply/divide rule. Rest/stop zeros, ½ and unit conversions are exact. Keep extra digits until the last line.
answer.commonMistake: Forgetting to square time, omitting the initial-velocity term, or confusing displacement with total distance.

companionQuestions.prompt: A puck moves at 54 km/h and stops over 50.0 m. Find acceleration.
companionQuestions.asking: Convert the initial speed, then use the stopping distance.

clues.explanation: Acceleration opposes the moving object while it slows. Its starting velocity is positive on this axis, so braking acceleration is negative. At rest, vf = 0 m/s.

steps.title: Write the known values
steps.text: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 15 m/s; vf = 0 m/s; Δx = 50.0 m. Convert 54 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 15 m/s. The conversion factors are exact.

steps.title: Choose the relationship
steps.text: vf² = vi² + 2aΔx

hints: This connects the two velocities, acceleration and displacement. Time is not in it, so you can solve without knowing how long the motion takes.
Convert 54 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 15 m/s. The conversion factors are exact.

a = (vf² − vi²) / (2 × Δd)
a = (0² − 15²) / (2 × 50.0)
Signed calculation: -2.25 m/s². Final: 2.3 m/s² backward.

repair.prompt: What does vf² − vi² require?
repair.explanation: Use the equation without time. Square each velocity separately, then rearrange for the one unknown before substituting signed values.

answer.reasoning: Take right/forward as positive; left/backward is negative. vi = 15 m/s; vf = 0 m/s; Δd = 50.0 m. This connects the two velocities, acceleration and displacement. Time is not in it, so you can solve without knowing how long the motion takes. a = -2.25 m/s² before final rounding. Final magnitude: 2.3 m/s² backward. The stated measurements limit this result to 2 significant figures. For a velocity difference, subtract first using the least decimal place; then apply the multiply/divide rule. Rest/stop zeros, ½ and unit conversions are exact. Keep extra digits until the last line.
answer.commonMistake: Treating vf² − vi² as (vf − vi)², forgetting the final square root, or using the wrong acceleration sign.

companionQuestions.prompt: A driver moving at 22.0 m/s reacts for 0.80 s, then brakes at 6.0 m/s². A deer is 40.0 m ahead. Find the stopping distance.
companionQuestions.asking: During the 0.80 s reaction time, the car is still moving at 22.0 m/s. Braking has not begun.

clues.explanation: The final velocity is zero. It is not the initial velocity.
Acceleration opposes the motion. If forward is positive, this acceleration is negative; a requested magnitude is positive.

steps.title: Separate reacting from braking
steps.text: During the 0.80 s reaction time, the car is still moving at 22.0 m/s. Braking has not begun.

steps.title: Work out the braking distance
steps.text: Take forward as positive. Braking acceleration is −6.0 m/s² and the final velocity is zero.

steps.title: Add the distances before rounding
steps.text: The car moves during both parts. Compare the total with the deer’s position, not just the braking distance.

steps.title: Use the distance to answer the situation
steps.text: The deer is only 40.0 m ahead. The ideal stopping distance is about 57.93 m, so the car cannot stop before that point.

steps.title: Round the final line
steps.text: The reaction and braking calculations are limited by 0.80 s and 6.0 m/s². Keep both distances unrounded when adding, then give the total to the nearest metre. It exceeds the deer’s 40.0 m position.

hints: During the 0.80 s reaction time, the car is still moving at 22.0 m/s. Braking has not begun.
Take forward as positive. Braking acceleration is −6.0 m/s² and the final velocity is zero.
companionQuestions.example:
d(reaction) = (22.0)(0.80) = 17.6 m
0² = 22.0² + 2(−6.0)Δd → Δd = 484 / 12 = 40.333… m
d(stop) = 17.6 + 40.333… = 57.933… m
57.93 m > 40.0 m
Stopping distance ≈ 58 m; the car cannot stop before the deer.

repair.prompt: Which distances make up the total stopping distance?

answer.commonMistake: Leaving out the reaction distance or applying braking acceleration before the driver starts braking.

checklist: Stopping distance ≈ 58 m; the car cannot stop before the deer.

repair.answer: Initial speed is twice the average speed

60 − 4.9t² = 20t − 4.9t² → 60 = 20t → t = 3 s.

reading.heading: Format
reading.text: Letter-sized white pages, one-inch margins, 12-point Times New Roman and single spacing. The title is centred about one-third down the title page; identifying fields go at lower right.

reading.heading: Report order
reading.text: Objective; Introduction; Materials; Procedure; Results; Calculations; Discussion; Conclusion; Literature Cited. Procedure and conclusions use impersonal past tense.

reading.heading: Results and discussion
reading.text: Tables need headings, units and instrument uncertainty. Graphs need axes, scale, caption and best fit. Show one sample of each calculation type, then table repeated calculations. Explain how each error changes the result.

reading.heading: Percent error
reading.text: Use |experimental − accepted| / |accepted| × 100%. It compares a measurement with a justified accepted value. Keep calculation precision until the final rounding; the sources do not establish a universal two-decimal rule.

reading.heading: Physical properties
reading.text: A physical property can be observed without changing chemical identity. Density does not depend on the amount of a substance; total mass does. Classify using the property being measured.

reading.heading: Vapour pressure and boiling
reading.text: Particles escape from a liquid and can return to it. In a closed container at equilibrium, evaporation and condensation have equal rates. Boiling begins when vapour pressure equals external pressure.

reading.heading: Phase changes on a graph
reading.text: Read axes and conditions first. In an idealized heating curve for a pure substance at fixed pressure, a flat region represents a phase change: energy changes particle arrangement while temperature remains roughly steady.

reading.heading: Use the definition for this section
reading.text: Hebden p.166–168 calls electrons in open shells reactable/valence electrons, gives noble gases zero reactable electrons, and defines valence (combining capacity) using unpaired electrons. This differs from counting all outermost-shell electrons.

reading.heading: Bonding and forces
reading.text: A metal/nonmetal pair commonly forms oppositely charged ions; two nonmetals commonly share electrons. The ionic bond is the attraction between ions after transfer. London forces act between particles, through temporary dipoles.

reading.heading: Three counts, three different questions
reading.text: Atomic number Z is the proton count. For a neutral atom electrons equal Z; an ion’s charge is protons minus electrons. Mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Nuclear charge is +Ze, independent of the electron count.

reading.heading: A worked model beside the real list
reading.text: For H₂O, 6 + 1 + 1 gives 8 valence electrons. Two O–H bonds use four electrons. The remaining four form two lone pairs on O. Each H counts two electrons and O counts eight. Use that count–draw–check method on the assigned molecules.

reading.text: Use the teacher’s section sequence, diagrams and examples. The links below open only the small idea needed for that part; the original notes remain at the teacher’s link.

reading.heading: Fossilization
reading.text: Burial can protect remains before they decay. Sediment may become rock. Soft bodies and organisms without rapid burial are less likely to be preserved.

reading.heading: Relative dating
reading.text: In undisturbed layers, lower layers were deposited first. Index fossils help match layers in different places; this gives order rather than an exact number of years.

reading.heading: Half life
reading.text: Each half-life halves the parent amount that is left. Count the halvings, then connect that count to elapsed time.

reading.heading: Early earth
reading.text: The Miller–Urey apparatus combines methane (CH₄), ammonia (NH₃), hydrogen (H₂) and water vapour (H₂O) with an energy source. Organic building blocks, including amino acids, can form through nonliving chemistry. This experimental mixture is a model, not proof of the exact ancient atmosphere, and producing these molecules does not create a living cell. Proteinoid microspheres are nonliving cell-like compartments with selective permeability.

reading.heading: Endosymbiosis
reading.text: Bacteria retained inside larger ancestral cells gave rise to mitochondria and chloroplasts. Three clues support this ancestry: bacterial-like DNA, bacterial-like ribosomes and division by binary fission. Oxygen-using bacteria connect to mitochondria; photosynthetic bacteria connect to chloroplasts. Explain how each clue supports the proposed origin.

reading.heading: Evolution patterns
reading.text: Name the pattern, then explain why the example fits. Similar features can evolve independently; interacting species can affect each other’s evolution.
